0.title: The Bible Book by Book
0.essay:
The Bible is one story told in sixty-six books. This study gives a short overview of each one: its setting, the shape of its message, where it points to Christ, and why it should move us to worship. Use it before you read a book, or when you want to see where a passage fits.

How each chapter works

Each chapter has four parts. Setting says briefly who wrote the book, when and to whom. Outline walks through the book in a few movements, with a sentence or two on each, so that you can see the flow of the argument or story. Christ in the book shows how it points to Jesus, for he said the Scriptures “bear witness about me” (John 5:39). And a closing section draws out why the book should lead us to worship.

One story

The Old Testament books follow the order of the English Bible: Law, History, Poetry and Wisdom, and Prophets. The New Testament follows the Gospels, Acts, the letters and Revelation. Behind them all is one plot: creation, fall, redemption and new creation, centred on Christ. “For all the promises of God find their Yes in him” (2 Corinthians 1:20).

Using it with the commentaries

Each book also has a full commentary in the app. This study is the map; the commentaries are the walk through the country. Read the outline first, then open the commentary.

For reflection

Which books of the Bible do you know least? Choose one, read its outline here, and then read the book itself this month.

1.title: Genesis: The Book of Beginnings
1.essay:
Genesis tells how everything began: the world, humanity, sin, the nations and the people of God. Above all, it begins the promise that runs through the whole Bible, that the offspring of the woman will crush the serpent’s head (Genesis 3:15).

Setting

Genesis is the first of the five books of Moses, written for Israel in the wilderness to tell them who their God is and where they came from. It covers the time from creation to Joseph’s death in Egypt.

Outline

1–2 · Creation. God makes all things by his word, and they are very good. Humanity is made in his image, male and female, to rule the earth and walk with him.

3–11 · Fall and spreading sin. Adam and Eve disobey, and death enters the world. Sin spreads through Cain’s murder, the corruption that brings the flood, and the pride of Babel. Yet grace persists: God promises a deliverer, saves Noah and makes a covenant with all creation.

12–25 · Abraham. God calls Abram and promises him land, offspring and blessing for all nations (Genesis 12:1–3). Abraham believes God, “and he counted it to him as righteousness” (Genesis 15:6). His faith is tested when he is told to offer Isaac.

25–36 · Isaac and Jacob. The promise passes, against all human expectation, to the younger son Jacob, a schemer whom God wrestles and renames Israel.

37–50 · Joseph. Joseph is betrayed by his brothers, sold into Egypt, and raised to power, so that he saves his family in famine. “You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good” (Genesis 50:20).

Christ in Genesis

Christ is the promised offspring of the woman and of Abraham (Galatians 3:16), the better Adam who obeys where Adam failed (Romans 5:14–19), and the true ram provided in Isaac’s place. Joseph, rejected by his brothers and exalted to save them, foreshadows him.

For worship

Genesis shows a God who creates by a word, judges sin, and keeps his promises through generations of failure. He is not shaken by human evil. He works through it for good.

For reflection

Where in your life do you need to trust, like Joseph, that God is working for good through what others meant for evil?

2.title: Exodus: The God Who Redeems
2.essay:
Exodus is the great story of rescue in the Old Testament. God hears his people groaning in slavery, delivers them from Egypt by mighty acts, makes a covenant with them at Sinai and comes to live among them.

Setting

Written by Moses, Exodus picks up the story about four centuries after Genesis, when Jacob’s descendants have become a great people enslaved in Egypt.

Outline

1–4 · Slavery and the call of Moses. Pharaoh oppresses Israel. God appears to Moses in the burning bush and reveals his name: “I AM WHO I AM” (Exodus 3:14).

5–15 · Plagues, Passover and the sea. Ten plagues show the LORD’s power over Egypt’s gods. At the Passover, the blood of a lamb protects Israel’s firstborn. God parts the sea and Israel sings his praise.

16–18 · In the wilderness. God provides manna, water and victory, though the people grumble.

19–24 · The covenant at Sinai. God gives the Ten Commandments and the laws of the covenant to a people he has already redeemed. The law is the shape of life for the saved, not the way to be saved.

25–40 · The tabernacle. God gives plans for a tent where he will dwell among them. Israel breaks the covenant with the golden calf, Moses intercedes, God reveals his glory and mercy (Exodus 34:6–7), and at last his glory fills the tabernacle.

Christ in Exodus

Christ is our Passover lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7), the greater Moses (Hebrews 3:1–6), the true bread from heaven (John 6:32–35) and the one in whom God “tabernacled” among us (John 1:14).

For worship

Exodus shows a God who hears, remembers and acts to save. He redeems first and then commands. And he wants to live with his people.

For reflection

How does knowing you were redeemed first change the way you obey God’s commands?

3.title: Leviticus: Holy to the LORD
3.essay:
Leviticus answers a burning question raised by Exodus: how can a holy God live among sinful people? Through sacrifice, priesthood and holiness. Its key word is “holy”: “You shall be holy, for I the LORD your God am holy” (Leviticus 19:2).

Setting

Leviticus records the laws God gave Moses at Sinai, in the year after the exodus, for the priests and the people.

Outline

1–7 · Sacrifices. Five offerings: burnt, grain, peace, sin and guilt. They express dedication, thanksgiving and, above all, atonement for sin through the death of a substitute.

8–10 · The priests. Aaron and his sons are ordained. When Nadab and Abihu offer unauthorised fire, they are struck down: God must be approached as he commands.

11–15 · Clean and unclean. Laws about food, childbirth, skin disease and bodily discharges teach Israel that every part of life is lived before a holy God.

16 · The Day of Atonement. Once a year the high priest enters the Most Holy Place with blood, and a second goat carries the people’s sins away into the wilderness.

17–27 · Holiness in everyday life. The Holiness Code covers sexuality, justice, love of neighbour (Leviticus 19:18), feasts, the Sabbath year and the Jubilee.

Christ in Leviticus

Christ is both the perfect sacrifice and the great high priest, who entered the true holy place “by means of his own blood, thus securing an eternal redemption” (Hebrews 9:12). Because of him, the food laws and sacrifices have been fulfilled.

For worship

Leviticus teaches us that sin is deadly serious, and God’s holiness is a consuming fire. It also teaches us that God himself provides the way back to him. That should humble us and fill us with gratitude.

For reflection

Do you take God’s holiness as seriously as Leviticus does? How does Christ’s sacrifice give you confidence to draw near?

4.title: Numbers: Faithful God, Faithless People
4.essay:
Numbers tells of Israel’s forty years in the wilderness, between Sinai and the edge of the Promised Land. A whole generation dies in the desert because of unbelief, yet God keeps his promise to bring their children in.

Setting

Written by Moses, Numbers takes its English name from the two censuses of Israel (chapters 1 and 26). Its Hebrew title, “In the wilderness,” fits it better.

Outline

1–10 · Preparing to march. The people are counted and organised around the tabernacle. The priestly blessing is given (Numbers 6:24–26), and the cloud leads them out.

11–14 · Rebellion. The people complain about food, Miriam and Aaron oppose Moses, and when the spies return from Canaan, the people refuse to enter. God sentences that generation to wander forty years.

15–25 · Wandering and judgment. Korah rebels and is swallowed by the earth. Moses strikes the rock in anger and is barred from the land. A bronze serpent heals those bitten by snakes. Balaam, hired to curse Israel, can only bless.

26–36 · A new generation. The people are counted again, Joshua is appointed, and the land is prepared for division.

Christ in Numbers

Jesus said, “as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up” (John 3:14). Christ is also the rock that followed Israel (1 Corinthians 10:4), and the star from Jacob that Balaam foresaw (Numbers 24:17).

For worship

Numbers warns us against unbelief, which Hebrews applies directly to Christians (Hebrews 3:7–19). It also shows God’s patience: he carries a grumbling people for forty years and does not abandon his promise.

For reflection

Where are you tempted to grumble against God’s provision, rather than trust his promise?

5.title: Deuteronomy: Love the LORD Your God
5.essay:
On the plains of Moab, at the edge of the Promised Land, Moses preaches his farewell sermons to a new generation. He renews the covenant and calls Israel to love God wholeheartedly: “You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your might” (Deuteronomy 6:5).

Setting

Deuteronomy means “second law”. It is not a new law, but the law of Sinai preached again, shortly before Moses’ death.

Outline

1–4 · Remember. Moses recalls God’s faithfulness and Israel’s failures in the wilderness.

5–11 · The heart of the covenant. The Ten Commandments are repeated, followed by the Shema (6:4–9), calls to love God, teach children and not forget him in prosperity.

12–26 · The laws of the covenant. Laws for worship, leaders, justice, war, family and care for the poor, showing how love for God works out in society.

27–30 · Blessings and curses. Obedience will bring blessing; disobedience will bring curse and exile. Yet God promises to circumcise their hearts so that they will love him (Deuteronomy 30:6).

31–34 · Moses’ last days. Joshua is commissioned, Moses sings and blesses the tribes, views the land from Mount Nebo and dies.

Christ in Deuteronomy

Jesus quoted Deuteronomy each time he resisted Satan in the wilderness (Matthew 4:1–11), succeeding where Israel failed. He is the prophet like Moses whom God promised to raise up (Deuteronomy 18:15; Acts 3:22). And he bore the curse of the law for us (Galatians 3:13).

For worship

Deuteronomy shows that God wants not merely outward obedience but love from the whole heart. And it shows our need for a new heart that only he can give.

For reflection

Moses warned Israel not to forget God when life became comfortable. Where might comfort be making you forget him?

6.title: Joshua: The LORD Gives the Land
6.essay:
Joshua tells how God brought Israel into the land he had promised to Abraham. The victories are his, the land is his gift, and the people must choose whom they will serve.

Setting

The book follows the conquest of Canaan under Joshua, Moses’ successor, in the generation after the exodus.

Outline

1–5 · Entering the land. God commands Joshua to be strong and courageous. Rahab hides the spies and is saved by faith. The Jordan parts, and the people are circumcised and celebrate Passover.

6–12 · Conquering the land. Jericho falls at a shout. Achan’s hidden sin brings defeat at Ai until it is dealt with. Campaigns in the south and north defeat the Canaanite kings.

13–21 · Dividing the land. The land is given to the tribes by lot, and cities of refuge are set apart. “Not one word of all the good promises that the LORD had made to the house of Israel had failed; all came to pass” (Joshua 21:45).

22–24 · Serving the LORD. Joshua renews the covenant and calls on the people to choose: “But as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD” (Joshua 24:15).

A hard question

The destruction of the Canaanites troubles many readers. Scripture presents it as God’s judgment on peoples whose sin had become complete after centuries of patience (Genesis 15:16), carried out at a unique moment in redemptive history. It was not a licence for ethnic violence, nor a pattern for the church, which fights not against flesh and blood (Ephesians 6:12).

Christ in Joshua

Joshua and Jesus are the same name, “the LORD saves”. Christ is the greater Joshua who leads his people into the true rest (Hebrews 4:8–10). And Rahab, a Canaanite saved by faith, appears in his family line (Matthew 1:5).

For worship

Joshua shows that God keeps every promise, and that he is holy, judging sin while saving all who turn to him, even from among his enemies.

For reflection

What promise of God do you need to trust as you face your own “Jericho” this week?

7.title: Judges: No King in Israel
7.essay:
Judges tells of a dark, repeating cycle in Israel’s early history: sin, oppression, crying out, and deliverance by a judge. Each time things get worse. The book ends with a refrain: “In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes” (Judges 21:25).

Setting

Judges covers roughly three centuries between Joshua’s death and the rise of the monarchy.

Outline

1–2 · Incomplete conquest. Israel fails to drive out the Canaanites, and a new generation arises “who did not know the LORD” (Judges 2:10). The cycle is set out.

3–16 · The judges. God raises up deliverers: Othniel, Ehud, Deborah and Barak, Gideon, Jephthah and Samson, among others. Each is flawed, and they grow more flawed as the book goes on. Gideon begins in faith but ends with an idol; Samson is ruled by his desires, yet God uses even his death.

17–21 · Total collapse. Two terrible stories show Israel’s moral and religious decay: idolatry in Micah’s house and the tribe of Dan, and the horrific abuse of a Levite’s concubine, leading to civil war.

Christ in Judges

The judges are imperfect saviours who point to a perfect one. The book’s cry for a king is answered, in part, by David, and fully by Christ, the King who saves his people from their sins and rules them in righteousness.

For worship

Judges shows the depth of human sin, even among God’s people, and the astonishing patience of God, who hears his people’s cry again and again.

For reflection

Where are you doing what is right in your own eyes, rather than submitting to Christ your King?

8.title: Ruth: The Kinsman-Redeemer
8.essay:
Set in the dark days of the judges, Ruth is a story of quiet faithfulness and kindness. A Moabite widow takes refuge under the wings of Israel’s God, and through her, God provides for a broken family and the line of King David.

Setting

The story takes place “in the days when the judges ruled” (Ruth 1:1). It ends with a genealogy leading to David.

Outline

1 · Emptiness. Naomi loses her husband and sons in Moab. Her daughter-in-law Ruth refuses to leave her: “Your people shall be my people, and your God my God” (Ruth 1:16).

2 · Kindness in the field. Ruth gleans in the field of Boaz, a relative of Naomi, who treats her with generosity.

3 · A request at the threshing floor. At Naomi’s urging, Ruth asks Boaz to act as her redeemer.

4 · Redemption. Boaz redeems Naomi’s land and marries Ruth. Their son Obed is the grandfather of David.

Christ in Ruth

Boaz is a picture of Christ, the kinsman-redeemer who pays the price to rescue those who cannot rescue themselves. And Ruth, a foreigner, is grafted into the line of the Messiah (Matthew 1:5), a sign that the gospel is for all nations.

For worship

Ruth shows God’s providence in ordinary events: a harvest, a chance meeting, a family law. He is at work even when he seems silent, turning emptiness into fullness.

For reflection

Where can you see God’s quiet providence at work in the ordinary details of your life?

9.title: 1 Samuel: The King the People Wanted
9.essay:
1 Samuel tells how Israel moved from judges to kings. It contrasts Saul, the king the people wanted, with David, the man after God’s own heart. “The LORD sees not as man sees: man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7).

Setting

The book covers the late eleventh century BC, from Samuel’s birth to Saul’s death.

Outline

1–7 · Samuel. God answers barren Hannah’s prayer with Samuel, who becomes prophet and judge. The corrupt priesthood of Eli falls, and the ark is captured and returned.

8–15 · Saul. Israel demands a king “like all the nations” (1 Samuel 8:5). God gives them Saul, who begins well but disobeys, and is rejected. “To obey is better than sacrifice” (1 Samuel 15:22).

16–31 · David and Saul. Samuel anoints the young shepherd David. David defeats Goliath, but Saul grows jealous and hunts him. David twice spares Saul’s life, refusing to seize the throne. Saul dies in battle against the Philistines.

Christ in 1 Samuel

Hannah’s song praises the God who lifts the lowly and speaks of “his anointed” (1 Samuel 2:10), the first time that word looks to a king. David, the overlooked shepherd who defeats the giant for his people, foreshadows Christ, the Good Shepherd who defeats sin, death and Satan.

For worship

1 Samuel shows that God raises up and brings down. He is not impressed by outward strength, but looks for humble, obedient hearts.

For reflection

Are you more like Saul, concerned with appearances, or like David, seeking God’s heart?

10.title: 2 Samuel: The Reign of David
10.essay:
2 Samuel tells of David’s reign over Israel: his triumphs, his terrible sin, and its consequences. At its centre is God’s covenant promise that David’s throne will last for ever.

Setting

The book covers David’s forty-year reign, around 1010 to 970 BC.

Outline

1–10 · David’s rise and triumph. David becomes king, first of Judah and then of all Israel. He takes Jerusalem and brings the ark there. God promises him an everlasting dynasty (2 Samuel 7:12–16).

11–12 · David’s sin. David commits adultery with Bathsheba and has her husband Uriah killed. The prophet Nathan confronts him, and David repents: “I have sinned against the LORD” (2 Samuel 12:13).

13–20 · Troubles in David’s house. As Nathan warned, the sword does not depart from David’s house: rape, murder, and Absalom’s rebellion. David flees and weeps over his son.

21–24 · Final words. David’s song of praise, his last words and his census, followed by plague and an altar on the site of the future temple.

Christ in 2 Samuel

The covenant with David points straight to Christ, “the son of David” (Matthew 1:1), whose kingdom has no end (Luke 1:32–33). Where David failed, Jesus is the righteous King.

For worship

2 Samuel shows that even the best of men need grace. It also shows that God keeps his promises despite our failures, and that real repentance is met with real forgiveness.

For reflection

Is there sin you need to confess, as David did, rather than hide?

11.title: 1 Kings: Glory and Division
11.essay:
1 Kings moves from the glory of Solomon’s reign to the division of the kingdom and the decline that followed. Kings are measured by one standard: did they walk in the ways of the LORD?

Setting

1 and 2 Kings were originally one book, written during the exile to explain why Israel and Judah fell. 1 Kings covers about 970 to 850 BC.

Outline

1–11 · Solomon. Solomon asks for wisdom and receives wealth and honour too. He builds the temple, and God’s glory fills it. But his many foreign wives turn his heart to other gods.

12–16 · The kingdom divided. Under Rehoboam the ten northern tribes break away under Jeroboam, who sets up golden calves. A succession of kings follows, most of them evil.

17–22 · Elijah and Ahab. In the days of Ahab and Jezebel, Elijah confronts Baal worship. On Mount Carmel fire falls from heaven: “The LORD, he is God” (1 Kings 18:39). Then the exhausted prophet flees, and God meets him in a low whisper.

Christ in 1 Kings

Solomon’s wisdom and kingdom of peace point to Christ, who is “greater than Solomon” (Matthew 12:42). The temple points to Christ, in whom God dwells with us (John 2:19–21). And Elijah’s ministry prepares for John the Baptist, who came “in the spirit and power of Elijah” (Luke 1:17).

For worship

1 Kings shows that wisdom and blessing do not keep us safe if our hearts turn away. It also shows that the LORD alone is God, and that he still has his faithful remnant.

For reflection

Solomon’s heart was turned slowly. What could be turning your heart from God by small degrees?

12.title: 2 Kings: Towards Exile
12.essay:
2 Kings tells the tragic end of both kingdoms. Israel falls to Assyria in 722 BC, and Judah to Babylon in 586 BC. God sent prophet after prophet, but the people would not listen.

Setting

The book covers about 850 to 560 BC, ending with the exiled King Jehoiachin released from prison in Babylon.

Outline

1–8 · Elisha. Elijah is taken up to heaven, and Elisha performs many miracles: raising a boy, healing Naaman, feeding a hundred.

9–17 · The fall of Israel. Jehu wipes out Ahab’s house but does not turn fully to God. The north sinks into idolatry, and Assyria destroys Samaria. Chapter 17 explains why: they “would not listen” (2 Kings 17:14).

18–25 · The fall of Judah. Good kings like Hezekiah and Josiah bring reform. Hezekiah trusts God when Assyria besieges Jerusalem, and the city is spared. Josiah rediscovers the Book of the Law. But Manasseh’s great evil seals Judah’s fate, and Babylon destroys Jerusalem and the temple.

Christ in 2 Kings

Elisha’s miracles of healing, raising the dead and feeding the hungry foreshadow Christ’s, and Jesus pointed to Naaman as a sign of grace to the nations (Luke 4:27). The book ends with a son of David still alive in Babylon, a small sign that the promise of a King has not died.

For worship

2 Kings shows that God is patient but not indifferent. Persistent sin brings judgment. Yet even in judgment, he keeps a thread of hope alive.

For reflection

God sent many warnings before the exile. Are there warnings in your life that you have been ignoring?

13.title: 1 Chronicles: The House of David
13.essay:
Chronicles retells Israel’s history for those who returned from exile. It focuses on David, the temple and true worship, to assure a discouraged people that God’s promises still stand.

Setting

1 and 2 Chronicles were originally one book, written after the return from Babylon, perhaps by Ezra or someone close to him.

Outline

1–9 · Genealogies. From Adam to the returned exiles, the lists show that God’s people have a continuous history and a place in his purposes.

10–12 · David becomes king. After Saul’s death, all Israel gathers to make David king.

13–17 · The ark and the covenant. David brings the ark to Jerusalem with joyful worship. God promises him a house, a dynasty that will last for ever.

18–29 · Preparing for the temple. David’s victories bring peace. He gathers materials, organises the priests, Levites and musicians, and charges Solomon to build the temple. He prays: “Yours, O LORD, is the greatness and the power and the glory and the victory and the majesty” (1 Chronicles 29:11).

Christ in 1 Chronicles

The genealogies lead to David, and David’s line leads to Christ. The promise of a son whose throne will be established for ever (1 Chronicles 17:12–14) is fulfilled only in him.

For worship

Chronicles calls a weak and small people to worship the great King and to trust that his purposes have not failed.

For reflection

David gave generously for a temple he would never see. What could you give to God’s work for the sake of the next generation?

14.title: 2 Chronicles: The Temple and the Kings of Judah
14.essay:
2 Chronicles follows the kings of Judah from Solomon to the exile, measuring each by his faithfulness to God and his care for the temple. It ends with a call to go up and rebuild.

Setting

Continuing 1 Chronicles, it covers about 970 to 538 BC, focusing on Judah rather than the northern kingdom.

Outline

1–9 · Solomon and the temple. Solomon builds and dedicates the temple, and God answers: “if my people who are called by my name humble themselves, and pray and seek my face and turn from their wicked ways, then I will hear from heaven” (2 Chronicles 7:14).

10–36 · The kings of Judah. The kingdom divides, and Chronicles follows Judah’s kings. Some seek the LORD and are blessed, such as Asa, Jehoshaphat, Hezekiah and Josiah. Others forsake him and suffer. Even wicked Manasseh repents in captivity and is restored. Finally Jerusalem falls, and the book ends with Cyrus’s decree allowing the exiles to return.

Christ in 2 Chronicles

The temple, where God put his name, points to Christ, the true temple. The pattern of repentance and restoration points to the grace he brings. And the hope of a faithful son of David is fulfilled in him.

For worship

2 Chronicles shows that God responds to humble repentance, even in the worst of sinners, and that true worship lies at the centre of the life of his people.

For reflection

Manasseh, the worst of kings, was restored when he humbled himself. Is there anything in your life too far gone for God’s mercy?

15.title: Ezra: Return and Rebuilding
15.essay:
Ezra tells of the return of the exiles to Jerusalem, the rebuilding of the temple and the reforming of the people under God’s word. God keeps his promise to bring his people home.

Setting

Ezra covers two periods: the first return under Zerubbabel from 538 BC, and Ezra’s own return around 458 BC. Ezra and Nehemiah were originally one book.

Outline

1–6 · Rebuilding the temple. King Cyrus of Persia allows the Jews to return, fulfilling Jeremiah’s prophecy. They rebuild the altar and lay the temple’s foundation. Opposition halts the work, but the prophets Haggai and Zechariah stir them up, and the temple is completed in 516 BC.

7–10 · Reforming the people. Ezra, a scribe who “had set his heart to study the Law of the LORD, and to do it and to teach his statutes and rules in Israel” (Ezra 7:10), leads a second return. He finds the people intermarrying with idolaters, and leads them in confession and repentance.

Christ in Ezra

The return from exile is a shadow of the greater redemption Christ brings, freeing his people from the exile of sin. The rebuilt temple waits for the one who would fill it with greater glory (Haggai 2:9).

For worship

Ezra shows God moving the heart of a pagan king to fulfil his purposes. He is sovereign over the nations, and he rebuilds what sin has destroyed.

For reflection

Ezra studied, did and taught God’s word, in that order. Which of those three do you most need to grow in?

16.title: Nehemiah: Rebuilding the Walls
16.essay:
Nehemiah tells how a cupbearer to the Persian king led the rebuilding of Jerusalem’s walls in fifty-two days, in the face of fierce opposition, and how the people renewed their covenant with God.

Setting

Nehemiah returned to Jerusalem around 445 BC, about thirteen years after Ezra. The two men worked together.

Outline

1–2 · Prayer and plans. Hearing that Jerusalem’s walls are broken, Nehemiah weeps, fasts and prays. The king grants his request to rebuild.

3–7 · Building through opposition. Families each build a section. Enemies mock, threaten and plot, but Nehemiah prays and organises guards. Inside, he confronts the rich who are oppressing the poor. The wall is finished in fifty-two days.

8–10 · Renewal. Ezra reads the Law to the people, who weep. Nehemiah tells them, “the joy of the LORD is your strength” (Nehemiah 8:10). They confess their sins and make a covenant.

11–13 · Reforms. Jerusalem is repopulated and the walls dedicated. But the people fall back, and Nehemiah must deal again with Sabbath-breaking, mixed marriages and neglect of the temple.

Christ in Nehemiah

Nehemiah is a leader who gives up comfort to rebuild God’s city. Christ gave up far more to build his church, a city whose walls cannot fall. The book’s ending, with the people backsliding, shows that walls and reforms are not enough. We need a new heart.

For worship

Nehemiah shows prayer and hard work together, and a God who gives his people strength and joy in the hardest tasks.

For reflection

Nehemiah prayed before he spoke to the king. Before your next difficult conversation, will you pray first?

17.title: Esther: The Hidden Hand of God
17.essay:
Esther never mentions the name of God. Yet every page shows his providence, as a Jewish orphan becomes queen of Persia and saves her people from destruction.

Setting

The story takes place in the Persian capital Susa, during the reign of Ahasuerus (Xerxes I, 486–465 BC), among the Jews who did not return to Jerusalem.

Outline

1–2 · Esther becomes queen. Queen Vashti is deposed, and Esther, raised by her cousin Mordecai, is chosen. Mordecai uncovers a plot against the king.

3–5 · Haman’s plot. Haman, enraged that Mordecai will not bow to him, gets the king to decree the destruction of all Jews. Mordecai urges Esther to act: “who knows whether you have not come to the kingdom for such a time as this?” (Esther 4:14). She risks her life to approach the king.

6–7 · The reversal. On a sleepless night the king reads of Mordecai’s loyalty and honours him. At Esther’s banquet, Haman’s plot is exposed, and he is hanged on the gallows he built for Mordecai.

8–10 · Deliverance. A new decree allows the Jews to defend themselves. They are saved, and the feast of Purim is established.

Christ in Esther

Esther risks her life to stand between her people and death. Christ did more: he gave his life to save his people. And God’s preservation of the Jews preserved the line from which the Messiah came.

For worship

Esther shows that God is at work even when he seems absent, turning coincidences into deliverance and reversing the plans of the wicked.

For reflection

Where has God placed you “for such a time as this”? What would it look like to act in faith there?

18.title: Job: Suffering and the Sovereign God
18.essay:
Job is the Bible’s great book on innocent suffering. A righteous man loses everything, his friends wrongly blame him, and God at last answers him, not with an explanation, but with himself.

Setting

Job lived in the land of Uz, probably in the age of the patriarchs. The author and date of writing are unknown. Most of the book is poetry.

Outline

1–2 · The test. In heaven, Satan claims that Job serves God only for what he gets. God allows him to take Job’s wealth, children and health. Job worships: “The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD” (Job 1:21).

3–31 · Job and his friends. Job curses the day of his birth. His three friends insist that suffering must be punishment for sin. Job protests his innocence and longs for a hearing with God. In the middle of his anguish he confesses, “For I know that my Redeemer lives” (Job 19:25).

32–37 · Elihu. A younger man argues that God uses suffering to teach and refine.

38–42 · The LORD speaks. God answers from the whirlwind with questions about creation that Job cannot answer. Job repents of speaking beyond his knowledge. God rebukes the friends and restores Job.

What Job does not mean

Job does not teach that all suffering is caused by personal sin. That was the friends’ error, and God says they had not spoken of him what is right (Job 42:7). Nor does it teach that the godly should never lament. Job’s honest complaint is not condemned; his presumption is.

Christ in Job

Job longs for an arbiter between God and man (Job 9:33) and a living Redeemer. Christ is both. He is the truly innocent sufferer, who was counted a sinner and vindicated by God.

For worship

Job teaches us to bow before a God whose wisdom is far beyond ours, and to trust him when we cannot trace him.

For reflection

Can you worship God, as Job did, even when he has not explained your suffering?

19.title: Psalms: The Prayer Book of God’s People
19.essay:
The Psalms are one hundred and fifty prayers and songs, covering the whole range of human experience before God: praise, thanksgiving, lament, confession, trust and longing. They teach us how to talk to God.

Setting

David wrote about half of them. Others came from Asaph, the sons of Korah, Solomon and Moses, among others. They were collected over centuries, finishing after the exile.

Outline

The Psalms are arranged in five books, each ending with a doxology.

Book 1 (1–41). Mostly psalms of David, many of them laments. Psalm 1 sets the theme: the blessed person delights in God’s law. Psalm 2 introduces God’s anointed King.

Book 2 (42–72). Psalms of the sons of Korah and David, including David’s great confession (Psalm 51), ending with a prayer for the king.

Book 3 (73–89). Darker psalms, wrestling with the prosperity of the wicked and the apparent failure of God’s promise to David (Psalm 89).

Book 4 (90–106). An answer: “The LORD reigns” (Psalm 93:1). God was Israel’s dwelling place before there were kings.

Book 5 (107–150). Praise for redemption, the great psalm of the word (Psalm 119), the Songs of Ascents, and a final crescendo: “Let everything that has breath praise the LORD!” (Psalm 150:6).

Christ in the Psalms

Jesus said that the Psalms speak of him (Luke 24:44). He is the anointed King (Psalm 2), the suffering one who cries, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Psalm 22:1), the risen one who will not see corruption (Psalm 16:10), and the priest-king at God’s right hand (Psalm 110). He prayed the Psalms, and he prays them with us.

For worship

The Psalms give us words for every season, and they always lead us back to God, even from the darkest places.

For reflection

Choose a psalm that fits your present mood, and pray it slowly to God today.

20.title: Proverbs: The Fear of the LORD
20.essay:
Proverbs is a book of wisdom for everyday life: work, money, speech, friendship, marriage and parenting. Its foundation is clear: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge” (Proverbs 1:7).

Setting

Most of the proverbs come from Solomon. Others come from wise men, Agur and King Lemuel. Hezekiah’s men collected some of them (Proverbs 25:1).

Outline

1–9 · A father’s appeal. Long speeches urge a son to choose wisdom over folly. Wisdom is pictured as a woman calling in the streets, present with God at creation, while folly is a seductress whose house leads to death.

10–29 · The proverbs of Solomon and the wise. Short sayings, usually in pairs, contrast the wise and the foolish, the righteous and the wicked, the diligent and the lazy.

30–31 · Agur, Lemuel and the excellent wife. The book ends with a portrait of a woman of strength who fears the LORD (Proverbs 31:10–31).

How to read it

Proverbs are general truths, not promises without exceptions. “Train up a child in the way he should go” (Proverbs 22:6) describes what usually happens, not a guarantee. Job and Ecclesiastes balance Proverbs by showing that life does not always follow the pattern.

Christ in Proverbs

Christ is “the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24), “in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2:3). The wisdom by which God made the world became flesh in him.

For worship

Proverbs teaches that all of life is lived before God, and that reverence for him is where wisdom begins.

For reflection

Which area of your daily life most needs God’s wisdom this week: your words, your work, your money or your relationships?

21.title: Ecclesiastes: Life Under the Sun
21.essay:
Ecclesiastes is an honest look at life without God at the centre. Work, pleasure, wisdom and wealth all prove to be “vanity”, a breath or vapour. Only in fearing God and receiving his gifts with joy does life make sense.

Setting

The author calls himself “the Preacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem” (Ecclesiastes 1:1), traditionally Solomon.

Outline

1–2 · The search. The Preacher tries wisdom, pleasure, great projects and riches. All are “vanity and a striving after wind” (Ecclesiastes 2:11), because death comes to all.

3–6 · Time, injustice and toil. There is a time for everything, and God “has put eternity into man’s heart” (Ecclesiastes 3:11). Yet injustice, oppression and loneliness remain. The best we can do is enjoy God’s gifts.

7–12 · Living wisely. Wisdom is better than folly, though it cannot answer every question. Enjoy life with the people you love. Remember your Creator in youth, before old age and death. The conclusion: “Fear God and keep his commandments, for this is the whole duty of man” (Ecclesiastes 12:13).

What it does not mean

Ecclesiastes is not a book of despair. It strips away false hopes so that we will look to God. Its repeated call to eat, drink and enjoy work is not hedonism, but gratitude for God’s gifts.

Christ in Ecclesiastes

The world was “subjected to futility” (Romans 8:20), and Christ came to redeem it. His resurrection shows that death, the great leveller of Ecclesiastes, is not the end, and so “in the Lord your labor is not in vain” (1 Corinthians 15:58).

For worship

Ecclesiastes teaches us to hold life loosely and God tightly, to enjoy his gifts without making them gods.

For reflection

What are you chasing “under the sun” that cannot satisfy? What gifts of God do you need to enjoy with gratitude?

22.title: Song of Songs: Love as Strong as Death
22.essay:
The Song of Songs is a love poem, celebrating the desire, beauty and faithfulness of a man and a woman. It shows that romantic and sexual love, within marriage, is a good gift of God.

Setting

The title links it with Solomon. It is a collection of love poems, sung by the woman, the man and a chorus of friends.

Outline

1–2 · Longing and delight. The lovers praise each other and long to be together. Three times the woman warns her friends “that you not stir up or awaken love until it pleases” (Song of Solomon 2:7): there is a right time.

3–5 · The wedding and union. A royal procession, the wedding, and the joy of married love, followed by a moment of separation and searching.

6–8 · Mature love. The lovers are reunited. The woman says, “love is strong as death… Many waters cannot quench love” (Song of Solomon 8:6–7).

Two ways of reading it

For much of church history, the Song was read mainly as an allegory of Christ and the church, or God and the soul. Most interpreters today, including many Reformed scholars, read it first as a celebration of human love in marriage. The best approach does both in order: it is first about marriage, and because marriage itself is a picture of Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:32), it also points beyond itself.

Christ in the Song

Christ is the bridegroom who loves his bride, the church, with a love stronger than death. He gave himself for her, and he delights in her.

For worship

The Song teaches us to thank God for the gift of married love, to guard it, and to marvel at the far greater love of Christ.

For reflection

How does the Song’s picture of faithful, delighted love shape the way you view marriage and Christ’s love for you?

23.title: Isaiah: The Holy One of Israel
23.essay:
Isaiah is the greatest of the prophetic books. It sees the holiness of God, the sin of his people, the coming judgment and a salvation so great that it reaches the nations and ends in new heavens and a new earth. At its heart is the Servant who suffers for the sins of others.

Setting

Isaiah prophesied in Jerusalem from about 740 to 700 BC, during the threat from Assyria. Many scholars divide the book between several authors. The New Testament quotes all parts of it as from Isaiah (John 12:38–41), and conservative scholars hold it to be one book from the prophet.

Outline

1–12 · Judgment and hope for Judah. Isaiah sees the LORD high and lifted up: “Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts” (Isaiah 6:3). He promises a child called Immanuel, and a Son who will reign on David’s throne (Isaiah 9:6–7).

13–27 · The nations. Oracles against the surrounding nations, ending with a vision of God’s final victory over death.

28–39 · Trust or fear. Woes against those who rely on Egypt, and the story of Hezekiah’s deliverance from Assyria.

40–55 · Comfort for the exiles. “Comfort, comfort my people” (Isaiah 40:1). God, the only Creator, will bring his people home through Cyrus. And his Servant will bear their sins (Isaiah 52:13–53:12).

56–66 · The new creation. God calls all nations to his house, promises an anointed one who brings good news to the poor (Isaiah 61:1), and ends with new heavens and a new earth.

Christ in Isaiah

Isaiah has been called the fifth Gospel. Christ is Immanuel, the Prince of Peace, the shoot from Jesse and the Servant who “was pierced for our transgressions” (Isaiah 53:5). Jesus began his ministry by reading Isaiah 61 and saying, “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing” (Luke 4:21).

For worship

Isaiah leads us to tremble before the Holy One, and then to rejoice in the One who was crushed for us.

For reflection

Read Isaiah 53 slowly. What does it tell you about what Christ did for you?

24.title: Jeremiah: The Weeping Prophet
24.essay:
Jeremiah preached for forty years to a nation that would not listen, warning of Babylon’s coming judgment. He was rejected, beaten and imprisoned. Yet through him God promised a new covenant, written on the heart.

Setting

Jeremiah ministered from about 627 to 586 BC, during the final decades of Judah, and saw Jerusalem fall.

Outline

1 · The call. God appoints Jeremiah as a prophet before he was born, and puts his words in his mouth.

2–25 · Warnings to Judah. Judah has forsaken “the fountain of living waters” for broken cisterns (Jeremiah 2:13). In the temple sermon (chapter 7), Jeremiah warns against trusting in the building while living in sin. His laments, often called his confessions, show his anguish.

26–45 · Conflict and the fall of Jerusalem. Jeremiah clashes with false prophets and kings. He writes to the exiles to settle in Babylon and seek its welfare. In the Book of Consolation (30–33) he promises restoration and a new covenant (Jeremiah 31:31–34). Jerusalem falls, as he had said.

46–52 · The nations. Oracles against the nations, including Babylon itself, and an account of Jerusalem’s fall.

Christ in Jeremiah

Jesus established the new covenant in his blood at the Last Supper (Luke 22:20). He is the righteous Branch of David (Jeremiah 23:5), and like Jeremiah, he wept over Jerusalem and was rejected by his own people.

For worship

Jeremiah shows a God who grieves over his people’s sin, judges them justly, and yet promises to give them a new heart.

For reflection

Jeremiah stayed faithful though no one listened. How do you measure faithfulness in your own service: by results or by obedience?

25.title: Lamentations: Grief and Hope
25.essay:
Lamentations is five poems of grief over the destruction of Jerusalem. It does not hide the horror. Yet at its centre is a flash of hope: “The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning” (Lamentations 3:22–23).

Setting

Written soon after Jerusalem fell in 586 BC, traditionally by Jeremiah.

Outline

1 · The deserted city. Jerusalem is pictured as a widow, weeping, with no one to comfort her.

2 · The anger of the LORD. God has acted as an enemy against his people because of their sin.

3 · Hope in the darkness. A man who has suffered God’s rod remembers his mercy, and waits quietly for his salvation.

4 · Then and now. The horrors of the siege are contrasted with Zion’s former glory.

5 · A final prayer. “Restore us to yourself, O LORD” (Lamentations 5:21).

The first four poems are acrostics, each verse or group of verses beginning with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet: grief given order, from A to Z.

Christ in Lamentations

Christ wept over Jerusalem and bore the wrath of God that Lamentations describes. Because he did, God’s mercies are new every morning for his people.

For worship

Lamentations gives us permission to grieve and words to pray in the ruins. It teaches that God’s faithfulness is greater than our darkest day.

For reflection

When grief comes, where do you take it? Lamentations takes it to God.

26.title: Ezekiel: The Glory of the LORD
26.essay:
Ezekiel was a priest exiled to Babylon. In astonishing visions he saw God’s glory leave the temple because of Israel’s sin, and then return to a new temple. God will give his people a new heart and a new spirit.

Setting

Ezekiel was taken to Babylon in 597 BC and prophesied there from about 593 to 571 BC.

Outline

1–3 · The call. Ezekiel sees the glory of God on a throne-chariot and is commissioned as a watchman.

4–24 · Judgment on Jerusalem. Through sign-acts and visions, Ezekiel shows why Jerusalem must fall. The glory of the LORD departs from the temple (Ezekiel 10). Each person is responsible for their own sin, and God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 18:23).

25–32 · The nations. Judgment on Israel’s neighbours.

33–39 · Restoration. God will be his people’s shepherd. He promises, “I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you” (Ezekiel 36:26). In the valley of dry bones, the Spirit gives life to the dead.

40–48 · The new temple. A vision of a new temple, from which a river flows to give life, and a city whose name is “The LORD Is There” (Ezekiel 48:35).

Christ in Ezekiel

Christ is the Good Shepherd promised in Ezekiel 34 (John 10:11). The new heart and spirit come through his Spirit. And the river from the temple points to the living water he gives (John 7:37–39; Revelation 22:1).

For worship

Ezekiel shows a God whose glory is holy, who will not live with sin, and who yet raises the spiritually dead to life.

For reflection

Where do you need the Spirit to breathe life into what feels like dry bones?

27.title: Daniel: The Most High Rules
27.essay:
Daniel and his friends live faithfully in pagan Babylon, and Daniel’s visions show the rise and fall of empires until God’s everlasting kingdom comes. The message is clear: “the Most High rules the kingdom of men” (Daniel 4:17).

Setting

Daniel was taken to Babylon as a youth in 605 BC and served under Babylonian and Persian kings until about 536 BC. Many scholars date the book to the second century BC, but conservative scholars hold that it comes from Daniel himself, as Jesus implies (Matthew 24:15).

Outline

1–6 · Faithful in exile. Daniel refuses the king’s food. He interprets Nebuchadnezzar’s dream of a statue representing four kingdoms, smashed by a stone. His friends refuse to bow to an idol and are saved in the furnace. Nebuchadnezzar is humbled. Belshazzar sees the writing on the wall. Daniel keeps praying and is saved from the lions.

7–12 · Visions of the future. Four beasts rise from the sea, but “one like a son of man” receives an everlasting kingdom from the Ancient of Days (Daniel 7:13–14). Further visions show the conflict between empires, a ruler who persecutes God’s people, the seventy weeks, and the final resurrection (Daniel 12:2).

Christ in Daniel

Jesus’ favourite title for himself, “the Son of Man”, comes from Daniel 7. He is the stone that becomes a mountain filling the earth, and the one who receives the everlasting kingdom. He is with his people in the fire.

For worship

Daniel shows that God rules over every empire and every king. Nothing in history is outside his control, and his kingdom will outlast them all.

For reflection

Daniel kept praying when it was dangerous. What would it cost you to be faithful in your workplace or culture?

28.title: Hosea: The Faithful Husband
28.essay:
God commands Hosea to marry a woman who will be unfaithful to him. His broken marriage becomes a living picture of Israel’s unfaithfulness to God, and of God’s persistent, redeeming love.

Setting

Hosea prophesied to the northern kingdom of Israel from about 755 to 715 BC, in its final years before Assyria destroyed it.

Outline

1–3 · Hosea’s marriage. Hosea marries Gomer, who leaves him for other lovers. Their children’s names announce judgment. Then God tells Hosea to buy her back and love her again, as God loves Israel.

4–13 · Israel’s unfaithfulness. The people have no knowledge of God. They worship idols, trust in foreign alliances and offer empty sacrifices. “For I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice, the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings” (Hosea 6:6).

14 · A call to return. “Return, O Israel, to the LORD your God” (Hosea 14:1). God promises to heal their faithlessness and love them freely.

Christ in Hosea

Christ is the faithful bridegroom who buys back his unfaithful bride at the cost of his own life. Matthew sees in Hosea 11:1, “out of Egypt I called my son”, a pattern fulfilled in Jesus (Matthew 2:15). Paul uses Hosea to show that God calls Gentiles “my people” (Romans 9:25–26).

For worship

Hosea shows the depth of God’s hurt at our sin, and the greater depth of his love, which will not let his people go.

For reflection

Where have you been unfaithful to God? Hear his call to return, and his promise to love you freely.

29.title: Joel: The Day of the LORD
29.essay:
A devastating plague of locusts becomes a warning of the coming day of the LORD. Joel calls the people to repent, and God promises to restore them and to pour out his Spirit on all flesh.

Setting

Joel prophesied to Judah. His date is uncertain; suggestions range from the ninth to the fifth century BC.

Outline

1:1–2:17 · Locusts and a call to repent. Locusts have stripped the land. Worse is coming: the day of the LORD. “Rend your hearts and not your garments. Return to the LORD your God, for he is gracious and merciful” (Joel 2:13).

2:18–32 · Restoration and the Spirit. God promises to restore “the years that the swarming locust has eaten” (Joel 2:25), and to pour out his Spirit on all flesh, sons and daughters, old and young.

3 · Judgment on the nations. God gathers the nations for judgment, and blesses his people with abundance.

Christ in Joel

On the day of Pentecost, Peter declared that Joel’s prophecy was being fulfilled, as the risen Christ poured out the Spirit (Acts 2:16–21). “Everyone who calls on the name of the LORD shall be saved” (Joel 2:32), and Paul applies this to calling on the Lord Jesus (Romans 10:13).

For worship

Joel shows a God who judges sin, calls for real repentance, and pours out grace far beyond what we deserve.

For reflection

Is your repentance a matter of outward show, or a heart torn open before God?

30.title: Amos: Let Justice Roll Down
30.essay:
Amos, a shepherd from Judah, was sent to the prosperous northern kingdom to denounce its injustice, empty worship and complacency. God will not accept worship from those who oppress the poor.

Setting

Amos prophesied around 760 BC, during the long, wealthy reign of Jeroboam II.

Outline

1–2 · Judgment on the nations. Amos condemns the nations around Israel, then Judah, and finally Israel itself for selling “the righteous for silver, and the needy for a pair of sandals” (Amos 2:6).

3–6 · Israel’s sins. Israel’s privilege increases its responsibility. The rich lie on beds of ivory while the poor are crushed. God hates their feasts: “But let justice roll down like waters, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream” (Amos 5:24).

7–9 · Visions of judgment and hope. Visions of locusts, fire, a plumb line and a basket of summer fruit announce the end. Yet the book closes with a promise: God will raise up the fallen booth of David (Amos 9:11).

Christ in Amos

At the Council of Jerusalem, James quoted Amos 9:11–12 to show that the inclusion of the Gentiles in the church fulfilled God’s promise to rebuild David’s house (Acts 15:15–17). Christ is the Son of David who brings justice to the poor.

For worship

Amos shows that true worship and justice belong together. God cares how we treat the poor, and he sees what we do on Monday as well as Sunday.

For reflection

Is there any gap between your worship and the way you treat people with less power than you?

31.title: Obadiah: The Pride of Edom
31.essay:
The shortest book in the Old Testament announces God’s judgment on Edom, which rejoiced when Jerusalem fell. Pride brings a fall, and the kingdom will belong to the LORD.

Setting

Obadiah probably wrote soon after Jerusalem fell to Babylon in 586 BC. Edom, descended from Esau, was Israel’s brother nation, yet it helped its enemies.

Outline

1–9 · Edom’s pride. Edom thought its mountain cities made it safe. “The pride of your heart has deceived you” (Obadiah 3). God will bring it down.

10–14 · Edom’s violence. Edom gloated over Judah’s disaster, looted the city and handed over refugees.

15–21 · The day of the LORD. “As you have done, it shall be done to you” (Obadiah 15). But Mount Zion will be saved, “and the kingdom shall be the LORD’s” (Obadiah 21).

Christ in Obadiah

The kingdom that Obadiah foresaw is the kingdom of Christ. And Edom’s gloating over a brother’s fall is the opposite of Christ, who wept over his enemies and died for them.

For worship

Obadiah reminds us that God sees how we treat others in their time of trouble, and that he alone will reign.

For reflection

Have you ever secretly rejoiced at the misfortune of someone you dislike? Confess it, and pray for them.

32.title: Jonah: The Reluctant Prophet
32.essay:
Jonah is sent to preach to Nineveh, the capital of Israel’s cruel enemy Assyria. He runs away, is swallowed by a great fish, finally obeys, and then sulks when God shows mercy. The book is about God’s compassion, and the hardness of his prophet’s heart.

Setting

Jonah prophesied in the reign of Jeroboam II, around 780 BC (2 Kings 14:25).

Outline

1 · Running from God. Jonah boards a ship going the other way. A storm comes, and the pagan sailors fear the LORD more than Jonah does. He is thrown overboard and swallowed by a fish.

2 · Prayer from the deep. Inside the fish, Jonah prays: “Salvation belongs to the LORD!” (Jonah 2:9).

3 · Nineveh repents. Jonah preaches, and the whole city, from king to cattle, repents. God relents from the disaster he had threatened.

4 · Jonah’s anger. Jonah is furious that God is “a gracious God and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love” (Jonah 4:2). God rebukes him with a plant and a question: should he not pity this great city?

Christ in Jonah

Jesus pointed to “the sign of the prophet Jonah”: as Jonah was three days in the fish, so the Son of Man would be three days in the earth (Matthew 12:39–41). Christ is the greater Jonah, who went willingly to death to bring salvation to the nations.

For worship

Jonah shows that God’s mercy reaches even our enemies, and that he patiently works on the hearts of his own reluctant servants.

For reflection

Who is your “Nineveh”, the person or group you would rather God did not save? Pray for them today.

33.title: Micah: Walk Humbly with Your God
33.essay:
Micah, a contemporary of Isaiah, condemns the corruption of Israel and Judah, but also promises a ruler from Bethlehem who will shepherd God’s people. He sums up what God requires: justice, kindness and humility.

Setting

Micah came from a small town in Judah and prophesied from about 735 to 700 BC.

Outline

The book moves three times from judgment to hope.

1–2 · Judgment and a remnant. Samaria and Jerusalem will fall because of idolatry and the theft of land from the poor. Yet God will gather a remnant.

3–5 · Corrupt leaders and a coming King. Leaders, priests and prophets serve for money. But in the latter days, nations will stream to God’s mountain. A ruler will come from Bethlehem, “whose coming forth is from of old, from ancient days” (Micah 5:2).

6–7 · God’s case and his mercy. God brings a lawsuit against his people: “what does the LORD require of you but to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God?” (Micah 6:8). The book ends in wonder: “Who is a God like you, pardoning iniquity?” (Micah 7:18).

Christ in Micah

The scribes quoted Micah 5:2 to tell Herod where the Christ would be born (Matthew 2:5–6). Christ is the ruler from Bethlehem whose origin is eternal, and the shepherd who brings peace.

For worship

Micah ends with a God who delights in steadfast love and casts our sins into the depths of the sea. There is no one like him.

For reflection

Which of Micah’s three requirements, justice, kindness or humility, do you most need God’s help with?

34.title: Nahum: The Fall of Nineveh
34.essay:
About a century after Jonah, Nineveh had returned to its cruelty. Nahum announces its final destruction. God is slow to anger, but he will not leave the guilty unpunished.

Setting

Nahum prophesied between the fall of Thebes in 663 BC and the fall of Nineveh in 612 BC.

Outline

1 · The LORD who avenges. “The LORD is slow to anger and great in power, and the LORD will by no means clear the guilty” (Nahum 1:3). He is a refuge for those who trust him.

2 · The fall of Nineveh. A vivid picture of the attack on the city.

3 · Woe to the bloody city. Nineveh’s violence and lies are exposed. All who hear of its fall will clap their hands.

Christ in Nahum

Nahum proclaims “good news” of peace for God’s people when their oppressor falls (Nahum 1:15). Christ brings the final good news, defeating the great oppressor, Satan, and bringing peace.

For worship

Nahum comforts those who suffer under cruel powers. God sees, and he will judge. His patience is not weakness.

For reflection

How does Nahum’s promise that God will judge evil free you from the need to take revenge yourself?

35.title: Habakkuk: The Righteous Shall Live by Faith
35.essay:
Habakkuk argues with God. Why does he allow injustice in Judah? And why would he use the even more wicked Babylonians to punish it? God’s answer leads the prophet from complaint to a song of trust.

Setting

Habakkuk prophesied shortly before the Babylonian invasion, around 605 BC.

Outline

1 · Two complaints. Habakkuk asks how long God will allow violence in Judah. God answers that he is raising up the Babylonians. Habakkuk is shocked: how can a holy God use them?

2 · God’s answer. The vision will come in God’s time. “But the righteous shall live by his faith” (Habakkuk 2:4). Five woes announce that Babylon too will fall. “The earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD as the waters cover the sea” (Habakkuk 2:14).

3 · A prayer of trust. Habakkuk recalls God’s mighty acts, and resolves to rejoice even if everything fails: “yet I will rejoice in the LORD; I will take joy in the God of my salvation” (Habakkuk 3:18).

Christ in Habakkuk

Paul quotes Habakkuk 2:4 to show that we are justified by faith in Christ (Romans 1:17; Galatians 3:11). It was this verse, through Romans, that opened the gospel to Luther.

For worship

Habakkuk teaches us to bring our hardest questions to God, to wait for his answer, and to rejoice in him even when we have nothing else.

For reflection

Could you say, with Habakkuk, “though the fig tree should not blossom… yet I will rejoice in the LORD”?

36.title: Zephaniah: The Day Is Near
36.essay:
Zephaniah announces the great day of the LORD, a day of wrath against all sin. But beyond the judgment he sees a purified people, and a God who rejoices over them with singing.

Setting

Zephaniah prophesied during the reign of Josiah (640–609 BC), probably before his reforms.

Outline

1 · Judgment on Judah. The day of the LORD is near, a day of wrath on idolaters and the complacent who say, “The LORD will not do good, nor will he do ill” (Zephaniah 1:12).

2 · Judgment on the nations. Seek the LORD, seek righteousness and humility, before the day comes.

3 · Purification and joy. Jerusalem too is corrupt, but God will purify a humble remnant. “The LORD your God is in your midst, a mighty one who will save; he will rejoice over you with gladness” (Zephaniah 3:17).

Christ in Zephaniah

The wrath of the day of the LORD fell on Christ at the cross for all who trust him. And in Christ, God is “in our midst”, rejoicing over his redeemed people.

For worship

Zephaniah shows both the terror of God’s judgment and the wonder of his delight in his people.

For reflection

Do you believe that God rejoices over you with singing, if you are in Christ? How would that change your day?

37.title: Haggai: Rebuild the House
37.essay:
The returned exiles had laid the temple’s foundation and then stopped, busy with their own houses. Haggai calls them to put God first and rebuild, promising that the latter glory will be greater than the former.

Setting

Haggai’s four messages are precisely dated to 520 BC, about eighteen years after the first return.

Outline

1 · Consider your ways. “Is it a time for you yourselves to dwell in your paneled houses, while this house lies in ruins?” (Haggai 1:4). The people obey and begin to build.

2:1–9 · Greater glory. The new temple seems poor compared with Solomon’s. But God says, “The latter glory of this house shall be greater than the former” (Haggai 2:9).

2:10–19 · Clean and unclean. Their work had been defiled by their disobedience, but from now on God will bless them.

2:20–23 · Zerubbabel. God will make Zerubbabel, of David’s line, like a signet ring.

Christ in Haggai

The greater glory of the second temple came when Christ, God in the flesh, walked in its courts. Zerubbabel appears in Jesus’ genealogy (Matthew 1:12–13), and the signet ring points to the King God has chosen.

For worship

Haggai calls us to put God’s kingdom first, and promises that he is with us in the work: “I am with you, declares the LORD” (Haggai 1:13).

For reflection

Have your own priorities crowded out God’s work? What would it mean to “consider your ways”?

38.title: Zechariah: Your King Is Coming
38.essay:
Zechariah encouraged the returned exiles with visions of God’s plans for Jerusalem and promises of a coming King, humble and riding on a donkey, who would be pierced, and in whom a fountain for sin would be opened.

Setting

Zechariah began prophesying in 520 BC, alongside Haggai. His later chapters may come from later in his life.

Outline

1–6 · Eight night visions. Horsemen, horns, a measuring line, the high priest Joshua given clean garments, a lampstand, a flying scroll and chariots: God will restore Jerusalem, remove sin and empower his people. “Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, says the LORD of hosts” (Zechariah 4:6).

7–8 · True fasting. God wants justice and mercy, not empty rituals. One day many nations will seek him in Jerusalem.

9–14 · The coming King. “Behold, your king is coming to you; righteous and having salvation is he, humble and mounted on a donkey” (Zechariah 9:9). The shepherd is rejected and valued at thirty pieces of silver. The people will look on him whom they have pierced and mourn (Zechariah 12:10). A fountain will be opened to cleanse sin, and the LORD will be king over all the earth.

Christ in Zechariah

Zechariah is quoted in the Gospels more than almost any other prophet in the passion narratives. Jesus rode into Jerusalem on a donkey, was betrayed for thirty pieces of silver, and was pierced (John 19:37). The struck shepherd is Christ (Matthew 26:31).

For worship

Zechariah shows a God who has planned redemption in detail and who will bring it about, not by human strength, but by his Spirit.

For reflection

Where are you relying on your own might rather than the Spirit of God?

39.title: Malachi: My Messenger
39.essay:
The last book of the Old Testament finds God’s people weary, cynical and careless in worship. Malachi rebukes them through a series of disputes, and promises a messenger to prepare the way of the Lord.

Setting

Malachi prophesied around 450–430 BC, probably close to Nehemiah’s time, when the temple was rebuilt but zeal had faded.

Outline

1:1–5 · God’s love. “I have loved you, says the LORD.” The people reply, “How have you loved us?”

1:6–2:9 · Polluted worship. The priests offer blind and lame animals. God’s name will be great among the nations, even if his own priests despise it.

2:10–16 · Broken faithfulness. The people marry idolaters and divorce their wives. “For the man who does not love his wife but divorces her, says the LORD, the God of Israel, covers his garment with violence” (Malachi 2:16).

2:17–3:5 · The messenger. God will send his messenger to prepare the way, and the Lord will come suddenly to his temple, to refine his people.

3:6–4:6 · Return to me. They are robbing God in tithes and offerings. A book of remembrance is written for those who fear him. The sun of righteousness will rise with healing, and Elijah will come before the great day.

Christ in Malachi

Jesus identified John the Baptist as the promised messenger and Elijah (Matthew 11:10, 14). Christ is the Lord who came suddenly to his temple, and the sun of righteousness. After Malachi, there were four hundred years of prophetic silence until John came.

For worship

Malachi calls us out of tired, half-hearted worship to give God our best, because his name is great among the nations.

For reflection

Is your worship of God wholehearted, or have you begun to give him what is left over?
